bank.title: Women's Health and Young Adults (RACP Written Exam)
bank.description: Twelve RACP Basic Physician Training written-standard questions (8 SBA, 4 CDP) covering women's health, obstetric medicine, and young adult medicine, mapped to RACP BPT and General and Acute Care Medicine curriculum standards.
sources: RACP Basic Training and General and Acute Care Medicine curriculum standards (topic mapping)
RHDAustralia ARF and RHD guideline (3rd edition, 2020)
Endocrine Society functional hypothalamic amenorrhea guideline (2017)
UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC 2025)

questions.source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (2017)
stem: Maya Chen, 23, a distance runner and physiotherapy student, presents with 14 months of secondary amenorrhoea and a recent navicular stress fracture. Her body mass index is 17.8 kg/m2, and she takes no regular medications.

Pregnancy, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid dysfunction, and hyperandrogenism have been excluded. Despite 6 months of structured nutritional rehabilitation and reduced training volume, she remains amenorrhoeic.
questions.lead: Which pharmacological regimen is MOST appropriate to protect her bone mineral density?

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly
options.why: Bisphosphonates are generally avoided in premenopausal women of childbearing potential due to prolonged skeletal retention and fetal risk, and they do not address hypo-oestrogenism.

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 30 microg
options.why: Common trap: Oral ethinyloestradiol undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism that suppresses insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and fails to reliably improve bone mineral density in functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea.

options.text: Medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks
options.why: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate further suppresses gonadotrophins and exacerbates hypo-oestrogenic bone loss.

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol monotherapy without progestogen
options.why: Unopposed systemic oestrogen in a woman with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma.

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol with cyclical oral progesterone
options.why: Physiological transdermal oestradiol bypasses hepatic first-pass IGF-1 suppression to improve bone mineral density, while cyclical progestogen protects the endometrium.

questions.keyPoint: In functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea with low bone mineral density refractory to nutritional restoration, transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progestogen protects bone without suppressing hepatic IGF-1.

questions.source: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC 2025, CoSRH); Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
stem: Sophie Williams, 26, a graphic designer, attends an ambulatory care clinic requesting reliable long-term contraception. She has a history of migraine preceded by scintillating scotomas and transient unilateral hand paraesthesiae.
She also has essential hypertension controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily, does not smoke, and plans to conceive in 3 years. Blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg and neurological examination is normal.
questions.lead: Which contraceptive option is MOST appropriate for her?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 20 microg
options.why: Common trap: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 (unacceptable risk) in migraine with aura at any age, because of ischaemic stroke risk, even at low ethinyloestradiol doses. Her controlled hypertension adds further risk (UKMEC 3).

options.text: Combined vaginal ring releasing ethinyloestradiol and etonogestrel
options.why: Non-oral combined hormonal contraceptives carry the same systemic oestrogen vascular and thromboembolic risks as combined oral pills and remain contraindicated in migraine with aura.

options.text: Cyproterone acetate 2 mg with ethinyloestradiol 35 microg
options.why: This oestrogen-containing preparation carries higher thromboembolic and arterial vascular risk and is contraindicated in migraine with aura.

options.text: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system
options.why: Progestogen-only long-acting reversible contraception avoids oestrogen-mediated ischaemic stroke risk in migraine with aura and hypertension while reliably preventing pregnancy during perindopril therapy.

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg taken weekly as ongoing prophylaxis
options.why: Ulipristal acetate is licensed solely for single-dose emergency postcoital contraception and is not safe or effective as routine maintenance contraception.

questions.keyPoint: Oestrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura and hypertension; progestogen-only long-acting reversible methods such as a levonorgestrel intrauterine system are safe and effective.

questions.source: Clinical practice guidelines for the care of girls and women with Turner syndrome (Eur J Endocrinol, 2024)
stem: Hannah O'Connor, 24, a postgraduate science student with mosaic Turner syndrome (45,X/46,XX), transfers from paediatric endocrinology to an adult general medicine clinic. She takes transdermal oestradiol 50 microg twice weekly with cyclical oral progesterone.

She is asymptomatic, normotensive (blood pressure 112/68 mmHg), and has a grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation and an ascending aortic diameter indexed to body surface area (ASI) of 2.1 cm/m2.
questions.lead: Which surveillance strategy is MOST appropriate for her cardiovascular risk?

options.text: Annual exercise stress echocardiography without cross-sectional aortic imaging
options.why: Stress echocardiography assesses inducible ischaemia rather than thoracic aortic dimensions and inadequately visualises the distal ascending aorta and aortic arch.

options.text: Cardiac MRI or CT aortography every 2 to 3 years with strict blood pressure control
options.why: Adults with Turner syndrome, a bicuspid aortic valve, and an ascending ASI above 2.0 cm/m2 require regular thoracic cross-sectional imaging (MRI or CT) and strict blood pressure control to prevent aortic dissection.

options.text: Discharge from specialist cardiology follow-up unless chest pain develops
options.why: Thoracic aortic dissection in Turner syndrome occurs at smaller absolute diameters than in the general population and typically presents without prodromal symptoms.

options.text: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in 10 years if she remains normotensive
options.why: Common trap: A 10-year surveillance interval is unsafe in a patient with both a bicuspid aortic valve and an indexed ascending aortic diameter exceeding 2.0 cm/m2.

options.text: Urgent referral for elective aortic root replacement
options.why: Premature; elective aortic surgery in Turner syndrome is generally considered when ascending ASI reaches 2.5 cm/m2 or greater, or with rapid dilatation or additional risk factors.

questions.keyPoint: Women with Turner syndrome require lifelong thoracic aortic surveillance with cardiac MRI or CT aortography, particularly when a bicuspid aortic valve or ascending aortic dilatation is present.

questions.source: American Thyroid Association guidelines for thyroid disease during pregnancy and the postpartum (2017), recommendations 52–53
stem: Priya Nair, 29, an accountant at 10 weeks' gestation in her first pregnancy, presents with palpitations, heat intolerance and 3 kg weight loss. She had radioactive iodine ablation 3 years ago for Graves disease. Six months ago her TSH was 1.6 mU/L on levothyroxine 100 microg daily. When the pregnancy was confirmed 5 weeks ago, the dose was increased to 150 microg daily.
Heart rate is 104 bpm, blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, and she has mild bilateral exophthalmos without palpable thyroid tissue.
questions.lead: What is the MOST important clinical implication of her elevated TSH receptor antibodies?

options.text: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis is confirmed and requires no fetal monitoring
options.why: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis is driven by human chorionic gonadotrophin, is TRAb-negative, and needs functioning thyroid tissue. High TRAb titres reflect persistent Graves autoimmunity.

options.text: Maternal propylthiouracil must be started immediately to treat maternal hyperthyroidism
options.why: Her thyrotoxicosis followed a 50% levothyroxine increase, with a normal TSH on the previous dose, so it reflects over-replacement and the dose should come down. Antithyroid drugs cross the placenta. They are reserved for confirmed fetal thyrotoxicosis, given with levothyroxine.

options.text: Prior radioactive iodine ablation prevents fetal thyroid dysfunction in pregnancy
options.why: Common trap: TRAb can persist for years after radioactive iodine ablation, even though the mother now needs levothyroxine, and still reach the fetus.

options.text: Transplacental IgG transfer can cause fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis
options.why: TRAb are IgG antibodies that cross the placenta and stimulate the fetal thyroid from about 20 weeks, even after maternal ablation. At more than 3 times the upper limit, ATA recommends fetal ultrasound surveillance, with TRAb repeated at 18–22 weeks and, if still raised, at 30–34 weeks.

options.text: TSH receptor antibodies cannot cross the placenta because they are IgM molecules
options.why: TRAb are IgG antibodies, which are actively carried across the placenta by neonatal Fc receptors.

questions.keyPoint: TSH receptor antibodies persist after thyroid ablation and cross the placenta as IgG. When they exceed 3 times the upper limit, monitor the fetus and repeat TRAb at 18–22 and 30–34 weeks for fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis.

questions.source: ESID Registry working definitions for the clinical diagnosis of inborn errors of immunity (2019)
stem: Liam Patel, 18, an apprentice electrician, is reviewed in the general medical clinic after admission for lobar Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia. Since he was about 10 months old he has had recurrent ear infections, sinusitis and pneumonia, treated with repeated antibiotic courses but never investigated. He also has intermittent non-bloody diarrhoea.
His maternal uncle died of meningitis aged 3 years. He takes no regular medications. Examination shows no palpable tonsils or cervical lymph nodes.
questions.lead: What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.text: Common variable immunodeficiency
options.why: Common trap: CVID usually begins after early childhood, and most patients have measurable circulating B cells that fail to mature into plasma cells. Infection from infancy, an affected maternal uncle and absent B cells point to a defect in B-cell development instead.

options.text: Selective IgA deficiency
options.why: Selective IgA deficiency means low IgA with normal IgG, IgM and B-cell counts. Here all three immunoglobulin classes are low.

options.text: Specific antibody deficiency
options.why: Specific antibody deficiency means poor polysaccharide vaccine responses with normal immunoglobulin levels and normal B-cell counts.

options.text: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia
options.why: Absent CD19+ B cells with low IgG, IgA and IgM, infections from about 10 months (when maternal IgG wanes), absent tonsils and an affected maternal uncle indicate X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK mutation). Milder cases can go undiagnosed into adolescence or adulthood.

options.text: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome
options.why: CD40 ligand deficiency blocks class switching, so IgM is normal or raised and circulating B-cell numbers are normal. Here IgM is low and B cells are absent.

questions.keyPoint: Absent circulating B cells with low IgG, IgA and IgM, infections from late infancy and an X-linked family history indicate X-linked agammaglobulinaemia rather than common variable immunodeficiency.

stem: Chloe Henderson, 27, a primary school teacher with classical phenylketonuria (an autosomal recessive disorder), attends a pre-conception clinic with her 28-year-old partner. Her partner is clinically unaffected, has no family history of phenylketonuria, and is unrelated to her.

She has maintained strict dietary phenylalanine control (plasma phenylalanine 180 µmol/L) for the past 6 months to prevent maternal phenylketonuria embryopathy. The birth incidence of phenylketonuria in their population is 1 in 10,000.
questions.lead: What is the approximate risk that their first child will be affected with phenylketonuria?

options.why: This reflects an incorrect square-root calculation of the mutant allele frequency.
This is the general population birth incidence and ignores that the mother is homozygous affected.

The affected mother transmits a mutant allele with probability 1; the partner's carrier probability is 2pq (2 x 1 x 1/100 = 1/50) and his transmission probability if a carrier is 1/2, giving 1 x (1/50) x (1/2) = 1/100.
This underestimates the risk by halving the transmission probability twice.

options.text: 1 in 50
options.why: Common trap: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (q2 = 1/10,000, so q = 1/100), 2pq (approximately 1/50) is the probability that the unaffected partner is a carrier, before multiplying by the 1/2 chance of transmitting the mutant allele.

questions.keyPoint: When one parent has an autosomal recessive condition (probability 1 of passing a mutant allele), the offspring's disease risk equals half the unaffected partner's population carrier frequency (2pq / 2 = q).

questions.source: RHDAustralia: 2020 Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (3rd edition)
stem: Jarrah Williams, 17, an Aboriginal Year 12 student from regional Victoria, is diagnosed with his first episode of definite acute rheumatic fever after presenting with migratory polyarthritis, fever of 38.6 °C, ESR 88 mm/hr, and a rising anti-streptolysin O titre.

Transthoracic echocardiography performed at diagnosis and repeated at 6 weeks shows structurally normal cardiac valves with no pathological regurgitation or rheumatic heart disease. He commences 4-weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.
questions.lead: What is the minimum recommended duration of secondary antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Five years after the last episode or until age 21 years, whichever is longer
options.why: Australian guidelines recommend secondary prophylaxis for a minimum of 5 years after the most recent episode of acute rheumatic fever without carditis or until age 21 years, whichever is longer (here until age 22).

options.text: Lifelong secondary antibiotic prophylaxis
options.why: Prophylaxis until age 40 years or lifelong is reserved for severe rheumatic heart disease or patients following valve surgery.

options.text: One year after resolution of arthritis
options.why: One year of prophylaxis is inadequate and leaves a high risk of recurrent Group A streptococcal infection and rheumatic carditis.

options.text: Ten years after the last episode or until age 21 years, whichever is longer
options.why: Common trap: Ten years or until age 21 years is the recommended prophylaxis duration for mild rheumatic heart disease, whereas acute rheumatic fever without rheumatic heart disease requires 5 years or until age 21 years.

options.text: Ten years after the last episode or until age 35 years, whichever is longer
options.why: Prophylaxis until age 35 years applies to patients with moderate rheumatic heart disease.

questions.keyPoint: Following a first episode of acute rheumatic fever without rheumatic heart disease, Australian guidelines recommend secondary benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis for at least 5 years or until age 21 years, whichever is longer.

questions.source: Australian Medicines Handbook: tamoxifen, drug interactions (CYP2D6 inhibitors)
stem: Rachel Kim, 39, a retail manager, takes adjuvant tamoxifen 20 mg daily following breast-conserving surgery and radiotherapy for oestrogen-receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma.
She develops moderate major depressive disorder and troublesome vasomotor hot flushes, and asks for pharmacological therapy.
questions.lead: Which antidepressant is MOST likely to reduce the effectiveness of her tamoxifen?

options.text: Citalopram
options.why: Citalopram is a weak CYP2D6 inhibitor with minimal clinically significant effect on tamoxifen bioactivation.

options.text: Desvenlafaxine
options.why: Desvenlafaxine has negligible CYP2D6 inhibition and is an effective option for both depression and vasomotor symptoms during tamoxifen therapy.

options.text: Escitalopram
options.why: Escitalopram exhibits weak CYP2D6 inhibition and does not substantially reduce active endoxifen concentrations.

options.text: Paroxetine
options.why: Paroxetine is a potent irreversible CYP2D6 inhibitor that blocks hepatic conversion of the prodrug tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen. In a large cohort, longer overlap with tamoxifen was linked to higher breast cancer mortality, and regulators advise avoiding it where possible.

options.text: Venlafaxine
options.why: Venlafaxine is a minimal CYP2D6 inhibitor and is frequently used alongside tamoxifen to treat depression and hot flushes.

questions.keyPoint: Potent CYP2D6 inhibitors such as paroxetine and fluoxetine impair bioactivation of tamoxifen to endoxifen and should be avoided where possible in patients receiving tamoxifen.

stem: Elena Papadopoulos, 31, a physiotherapist, gravida 1 para 0 at 33 weeks' gestation, presents to the emergency department with severe frontal headache, visual blurring, and right upper quadrant pain. She has no prior medical history and takes pregnancy multivitamins only.

Blood pressure is 172/114 mmHg on repeated readings 15 minutes apart, heart rate is 88 bpm, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. She has 3+ pitting lower limb oedema, brisk patellar reflexes, and 3 beats of ankle clonus. Cardiotocography shows a reassuring fetal heart rate pattern.
questions.lead: Which THREE management steps are MOST appropriate to initiate immediately?

options.text: Administer intravenous ergometrine to prevent postpartum haemorrhage
options.why: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy because it causes severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis.

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by maintenance infusion
options.why: Critical: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological signs (severe headache, visual disturbance, clonus) requires immediate intravenous magnesium sulfate (4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour) for eclampsia prevention.

options.text: Administer oral immediate-release nifedipine or intravenous labetalol to lower blood pressure
options.why: Acute severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic >= 160 mmHg or diastolic >= 110 mmHg) requires urgent controlled blood pressure reduction using oral immediate-release nifedipine, intravenous labetalol, or intravenous hydralazine.

options.text: Commence intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion as first-line antihypertensive therapy
options.why: Sodium nitroprusside is avoided in pregnancy due to fetal cyanide toxicity and unpredictable maternal hypotension.

options.text: Initiate oral ramipril 5 mg daily for long-term renoprotection
options.why: ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic throughout pregnancy, causing fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios.

options.text: Notify senior obstetric and neonatal teams to plan expedited delivery after maternal stabilisation
options.why: Definitive management of severe pre-eclampsia complicated by HELLP features and neurological irritability at 33 weeks is expedited delivery once maternal blood pressure and seizure prophylaxis are stabilised.

options.text: Restrict intravenous fluid resuscitation to a 1000 mL crystalloid bolus
options.why: Rapid crystalloid bolus administration in pre-eclampsia precipitates acute pulmonary oedema due to endothelial capillary leak; total fluid intake should be restricted to approximately 80 mL/hour.

options.text: Target a blood pressure below 100/60 mmHg within 30 minutes
options.why: Excessive or precipitous blood pressure lowering impairs uteroplacental perfusion and causes fetal hypoxia; the initial target is 130–150 / 80–100 mmHg.

questions.keyPoint: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological irritability and HELLP features requires immediate intravenous magnesium sulfate, urgent controlled antihypertensive therapy (nifedipine or labetalol), fluid restriction, and multidisciplinary planning for delivery after stabilisation.

questions.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 37b: Thromboembolic disease in pregnancy and the puerperium, acute management (2015)
stem: Nadia Al-Mansoor, 28, a marketing coordinator, gravida 2 para 1 at 35 weeks' gestation, presents with 5 days of progressive exertional dyspnoea and 2 days of painful left calf swelling. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

Temperature is 37.3 °C, blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 96 bpm, respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Her left mid-calf circumference measures 2.5 cm greater than the right. Resting 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia, and a shielded chest radiograph is normal.
questions.lead: Which THREE clinical decisions are MOST appropriate now?

options.text: Arrange bilateral lower limb compression duplex ultrasonography as the initial imaging test
options.why: Critical: In a pregnant woman with suspected pulmonary embolism and unilateral leg symptoms, bilateral compression duplex ultrasonography is the initial test of choice because confirming deep vein thrombosis establishes the diagnosis and indication for full anticoagulation without ionising radiation.

options.text: Commence oral rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily as an outpatient
options.why: Direct oral anticoagulants cross the placenta and are contraindicated in pregnancy due to reproductive toxicity and fetal haemorrhage.

options.text: Commence oral warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0 to 3.0
options.why: Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes fetal intracranial haemorrhage in late pregnancy; low-molecular-weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice.

options.text: Commence therapeutic-dose subcutaneous enoxaparin while awaiting diagnostic confirmation
options.why: With high clinical suspicion of pregnancy-associated venous thromboembolism, empirical therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin should be commenced immediately unless contraindicated while imaging is arranged.

options.text: Obtain baseline full blood count, coagulation profile, and renal function before anticoagulation
options.why: Baseline haemoglobin, platelet count, coagulation studies, and renal function are required to verify safe dosing and establish reference values prior to initiating therapeutic anticoagulation.

options.text: Order a serum D-dimer to exclude venous thromboembolism without imaging
options.why: Physiological elevation of D-dimer throughout pregnancy, especially in the third trimester, gives poor specificity and cannot safely exclude venous thromboembolism.

options.text: Perform immediate CT pulmonary angiography before lower limb ultrasound
options.why: CT pulmonary angiography delivers ionising radiation to proliferating maternal breast tissue and should be deferred if lower limb duplex ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis.

options.text: Place an inferior vena cava filter prior to anticoagulation
options.why: Inferior vena cava filters are not indicated for routine pregnancy-associated venous thromboembolism and are reserved for acute thrombosis with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation.

questions.keyPoint: In pregnant patients with suspected pulmonary embolism and lower limb signs, commence empirical therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin after baseline bloods and perform bilateral lower limb compression duplex ultrasonography before radiation-based chest imaging.

questions.source: ECCO guidelines on therapeutics in ulcerative colitis: medical and surgical treatment (2022)
stem: Zoe Papadimitriou, 18, a university student with pancolonic ulcerative colitis who recently transitioned from paediatric gastroenterology services, is on day 8 of admission for acute severe ulcerative colitis. She failed 3 days of intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily and received rescue infliximab 5 mg/kg on day 4.

Today she passes 11 bloody stools per 24 hours with diffuse abdominal tenderness, temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 108 bpm, and blood pressure 110/68 mmHg. Stool PCR, Clostridioides difficile toxin, and colonic biopsies for cytomegalovirus are negative. Supine abdominal radiograph shows a transverse colon diameter of 4.6 cm with mucosal islands.
questions.lead: Which THREE management actions are MOST appropriate now?

options.text: Add oral ciclosporin 2 mg/kg twice daily as sequential third-line salvage therapy
options.why: Sequential third-line immunosuppressive rescue with ciclosporin after failed infliximab carries high rates of severe opportunistic infection and mortality without reliably avoiding surgery.

options.text: Administer prophylactic-dose subcutaneous enoxaparin daily
options.why: Hospitalised patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis have a markedly increased risk of venous thromboembolism and require daily pharmacological thromboprophylaxis.

options.text: Commence total parenteral nutrition and continue intravenous hydrocortisone for 10 more days
options.why: Prolonging ineffective corticosteroid therapy beyond 7 to 10 days increases postoperative sepsis and mortality, and enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral nutrition when the gut is functional.

options.text: Involve a stomal therapy nurse and engage the young adult directly in shared surgical decision-making
options.why: An 18-year-old adult has full legal decision-making capacity; early stomal therapy education and direct, empathetic shared decision-making support informed consent and psychosocial adaptation.

options.text: Obtain written consent from her parents before discussing colectomy with the patient
options.why: At age 18 in Australia, the patient is a legal adult with autonomous decision-making capacity; seeking parental consent instead of the patient's consent breaches autonomy and confidentiality.

options.text: Perform an urgent full colonoscopy to reassess endoscopic severity
options.why: Full colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute severe ulcerative colitis because of the high risk of colonic perforation.

options.text: Prescribe oral loperamide 4 mg after each loose bowel motion
options.why: Antimotility agents are contraindicated in acute severe ulcerative colitis because they can precipitate toxic megacolon.

options.text: Refer urgently for subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy
options.why: Critical: Failure of second-line medical rescue therapy (infliximab) following intravenous corticosteroids in acute severe ulcerative colitis mandates urgent subtotal colectomy to prevent toxic megacolon, perforation, and death.

questions.keyPoint: Acute severe ulcerative colitis refractory to intravenous corticosteroids and rescue infliximab requires urgent subtotal colectomy, thromboprophylaxis, and direct shared decision-making with the young adult patient.

questions.source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for Use in Primary Care (ASHM): Proctitis
stem: Ethan Nguyen, 21, a hospitality worker, presents with 4 days of severe anorectal pain, tenesmus, mucopurulent rectal discharge, and scant rectal bleeding. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 12 days ago and is not taking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.

He has no diarrhoea or systemic fever. Examination shows shallow perianal erosions and tender bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Anorectal swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis (including lymphogranuloma venereum typing), Mycoplasma genitalium, and herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR have been collected.
questions.lead: Which THREE actions are MOST appropriate while awaiting swab results?

options.text: Administer empirical ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly, oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, and oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily
options.why: Critical: Australian STI guidelines recommend immediate empirical syndromic treatment covering gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose), chlamydia/LGV (doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days), and HSV proctitis (valaciclovir 500 mg BD for 7 days) before PCR results return.

options.text: Advise the patient that he is legally required to notify his employer of his STI diagnosis
options.why: There is no legal or public health requirement to disclose an STI to an employer, and doing so violates patient confidentiality.

options.text: Arrange HIV fourth-generation antigen/antibody testing, syphilis serology, and hepatitis A, B, and C screening
options.why: Anorectal mucosal inflammation and ulceration substantially increase HIV and syphilis acquisition risk; comprehensive blood-borne virus and syphilis serology is required at baseline and repeated after the window period.

options.text: Commence immediate 28-day HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
options.why: HIV PEP is only indicated within 72 hours of a high-risk exposure; at 12 days post-exposure, PEP is ineffective and HIV testing followed by PrEP counselling once HIV-negative is appropriate.

options.text: Counsel the patient to abstain from sexual contact until treatment is completed and symptoms resolve, and initiate partner notification
options.why: Abstaining from sexual activity until symptom resolution and completion of antimicrobial therapy prevents reinfection and onward transmission, alongside confidential partner notification.

options.text: Defer antimicrobial therapy until nucleic acid amplification results confirm the pathogen
options.why: Delaying empirical treatment prolongs severe pain, increases the risk of anorectal stricture or fistula in lymphogranuloma venereum, and enables ongoing transmission.

options.text: Prescribe single-dose oral azithromycin 1 g monotherapy
options.why: Azithromycin monotherapy fails to cover gonococcal proctitis, provides inadequate duration for lymphogranuloma venereum, and has no activity against HSV.

options.text: Refer for urgent colonoscopy prior to starting antimicrobial therapy
options.why: Colonoscopy is unnecessary prior to empirical STI therapy and risks mucosal trauma in acute ulcerative proctitis.

questions.keyPoint: Suspected sexually transmitted infectious proctitis requires immediate empirical coverage for gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone), chlamydia/LGV (21 days of doxycycline), and HSV (valaciclovir), alongside HIV/syphilis screening, abstinence advice, and partner notification.
